sec.title: Objective
sec.p: To report updated results of the phase 3 PHILA trial, which evaluated the efficacy and safety of pyrotinib or placebo in combination with trastuzumab and docetaxel in patients with untreated human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) positive metastatic breast cancer.

sec.title: Design
sec.p: Multicentre, double blind, randomised, placebo controlled phase 3 trial.

sec.title: Setting
sec.p: 40 centres in China, 6 May 2019 to 17 January 2022.

sec.title: Participants
sec.p: 590 female patients with untreated HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer.

sec.title: Interventions
sec.p: Eligible patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive either the irreversible pan-HER inhibitor pyrotinib (400 mg orally once daily) or placebo, both in combination with intravenous trastuzumab (8 mg/kg for the first cycle, then 6 mg/kg in subsequent cycles) and docetaxel (75 mg/m2) on day 1 of each 21 day treatment cycle.

sec.title: Main outcome measure
sec.p: The primary endpoint was investigator assessed progression-free survival.

sec.title: Results
sec.p: 590 patients were randomised and received treatment (297 in the pyrotinib group and 293 in the placebo group). As of 30 April 2024, during a median follow-up of 35.7 months in the pyrotinib group and 34.3 months in the placebo group, 59 (20%) and 87 (30%) patients died, respectively. Overall survival was longer in the pyrotinib group (hazard ratio 0.64 (95% confidence interval (CI) 0.46 to 0.89); nominal one-sided P=0.004). At end of follow-up, neither group had reached the median overall survival. Improvement in progression-free survival in the pyrotinib group was maintained (22.1 months (95% CI 19.3 to 27.8) v 10.5 months (9.5 to 12.4), hazard ratio 0.44 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.53); nominal one sided P<0.001). Adverse event profiles remained consistent with the interim analysis for type, frequency, and severity. After discontinuation of docetaxel, the overall incidence of adverse events decreased substantially. As of 30 May 2025, with a median follow-up of 45.5 months, the pyrotinib based regimen showed consistent and prolonged survival benefit.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The updated analysis of the phase 3 PHILA trial confirmed the superiority of pyrotinib in combination with trastuzumab and docetaxel over placebo in combination with trastuzumab and docetaxel in sustaining longer progression-free survival and improving overall survival for initial treatment of HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer. The safety profile remained consistent with interim findings, with no new safety signals identified during extended follow-up. This analysis reinforces the efficacy of this dual anti-HER2 (pyrotinib plus trastuzumab) regimen as an effective treatment strategy for this patient population.

sec.title: Trial registration
sec.p: ClinicalTrials.gov NCT03863223.

sec.title: Introduction
sec.p: Breast cancer remains a major health concern worldwide, with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 (HER2) positivity representing a distinct subtype associated with rapid progression of disease and poor prognosis.1 2 The overexpression or amplification of HER2 in breast cancer has been identified as a key driver of tumorigenesis and metastasis, making it a pivotal target for treatment intervention in patients with HER2 positive breast cancer. Dual anti-HER2 treatment, which combines two distinct components targeting HER2 with complementary mechanisms of action, has emerged as a cornerstone in the treatment of HER2 positive breast cancer.3 4 5 6 7 This approach aims to provide a more comprehensive blockade of HER2 signalling pathways, surpassing the efficacy achieved with single agent treatments. Among the dual anti-HER2 regimens, the combination of pertuzumab and trastuzumab along with docetaxel is the established standard of care for the initial treatment of patients with HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer, based on the landmark Clinical Evaluation of Pertuzumab and Trastuzumab (CLEOPATRA) study.5 8 9 10 11 This trial reported a median progression-free survival of 18.5 months in the pertuzumab, trastuzumab, and docetaxel group compared with 12.4 months in the placebo, trastuzumab, and docetaxel group (hazard ratio 0.62).

In recent years, the development of novel agents targeting HER2 has expanded the treatment options for HER2 positive breast cancer. Pyrotinib, a small molecule, irreversible, pan-HER receptor tyrosine kinase inhibitor has shown promising antitumour activity in both single agent and combination treatment settings.12 13 14 15 16 17 18 By targeting not only HER2 but also epidermal growth factor receptor (EGFR/HER1) and HER4, pyrotinib offers a unique mechanism of action that may lead to sustained inhibition of HER signalling and enhanced antitumour effects compared with reversible HER2 targeted tyrosine kinase inhibitors.19

The phase 3 PHILA trial has provided critical insights into the efficacy and safety of pyrotinib based regimens in the initial treatment of HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer. In the interim analysis of the trial, the combination of pyrotinib, trastuzumab, and docetaxel showed superior progression-free survival compared with placebo, trastuzumab, and docetaxel (median 24.3 v 10.4 months, hazard ratio 0.41), with acceptable toxicity profiles.20 This phase 3 trial showed the progression-free survival benefits of dual HER2 inhibition using a combination of a monoclonal antibody and a small molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor as the initial treatment for HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer. Based on this result, in April 2023, the China National Medical Products Administration approved this pyrotinib based regimen as an initial treatment for HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer. Although the interim analysis of the PHILA (PHase 3,Randomized, Double-blinded, Placebo-controlled Study to Evaluate Efficacy and Safety of PyrotInib Plus Trastuzumab and DocetaxeL Versus PlAcebo Plus Trastuzumab and Docetaxel in Patients With HER2 Positive MBC) trial showed promising results in terms of progression-free survival, the data for overall survival remained preliminary. Here, we present the prespecified final analysis of progression-free survival results, including overall survival, duration of response, and safety results after a longer follow-up period, as well as long term survival outcomes. This extended analysis aims to provide a more comprehensive understanding of the long term benefits and risks associated with the use of pyrotinib in combination with trastuzumab and docetaxel in the initial treatment of HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer.

sec.title: Study design and participants
sec.p: The PHILA trial was a multicentre, double blind, randomised controlled phase 3 study conducted at 40 centres in China. Full details of the study are reported elsewhere.20

Participants aged 18 to 75 years with histologically confirmed HER2 positive recurrent or metastatic breast cancer, who had not received the treatment for this stage of the disease were eligible. Other inclusion criteria included measurable lesions according to the Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors 1.1, Eastern Cooperative Oncology Group performance status (0 representing being fully active or 1 representing ability to carry out light or sedentary work),21 and adequate organ function.

Exclusion criteria included a history of anti-HER2 treatment for recurrent or metastatic breast cancer (excluding neoadjuvant or adjuvant trastuzumab use), a disease-free interval of less than 12 months from completion of previous systemic treatment in the neoadjuvant or adjuvant setting, central nervous system metastases, other malignancies, and left ventricular ejection fraction less than 50%. All patients provided written informed consent.

sec.title: Procedures
sec.p: Patients were randomly assigned in a 1:1 ratio to receive either oral pyrotinib (400 mg once daily) or placebo, both combined with intravenous trastuzumab (8 mg/kg in treatment cycle 1 and 6 mg/kg in subsequent cycles) and docetaxel on day 1 of each 21 day treatment cycle. Randomisation was done through a centralised interactive web response system. Stratification factors included previous use of trastuzumab in neoadjuvant or adjuvant therapy (yes v no) and hormone receptor status (oestrogen receptor positive and/or progesterone receptor positive v oestrogen receptor negative and progesterone receptor negative). Patients, investigators, and the sponsor were blinded to treatment allocation.

Treatment continued until disease progression, unacceptable toxicity, withdrawal of consent, decision of the investigator, or death. To manage toxicity, dose reductions of pyrotinib were allowed in a stepwise manner, from 400 mg to 320 mg, then to 240 mg. Reduction of trastuzumab dose was allowed only if weight loss exceeded 10%. Docetaxel dose could be reduced to a minimum of 60 mg/m2. Patients were required to receive at least six cycles of docetaxel. Secondary prophylaxis for diarrhoea was allowed during pyrotinib or placebo treatment. Patients who experienced an interruption to treatment or delay of study drugs (pyrotinib/placebo, trastuzumab, docetaxel) as a result of diarrhoea could receive prophylactic oral loperamide hydrochloride at a maximum daily dose of 16 mg, after investigator assessment. For patients with severe diarrhoea, oral or intravenous electrolyte replacement could be administered as clinically indicated. Crossover treatment was not allowed in this study. Concurrent use of endocrine treatment was also not allowed for patients with HER2 positive or hormone receptor positive disease.

Tumour assessments were conducted at baseline, every three treatment cycles, then every four cycles after the first 24 cycles using computed tomography or magnetic resonance imaging, with responses evaluated by both investigators and an independent review committee following Response Evaluation Criteria in Solid Tumors 1.1 criteria. Regular monitoring of laboratory assessments, 12 lead electrocardiography, and monitoring of vital signs were done every cycle and echocardiography every 12 weeks. Assessments for adverse events were performed throughout the treatment period and up to 28 days post-treatment. Adverse events were classified according to the Medical Dictionary for Regulatory Activities version 26 and graded according to the National Cancer Institute Common Terminology Criteria for Adverse Events version 4.03.

sec.title: Outcomes
sec.p: The primary endpoint of the study was progression-free survival, defined as the time from randomisation to the first documented radiographic progression or death from any cause, whichever occurred first, as assessed by the investigator. Secondary endpoints included progression-free survival as assessed by an independent review committee, overall survival (defined as the time from randomisation to death from any cause), objective response rate (the proportion of patients with a best overall response of complete or partial response), duration of response (the time from the first complete or partial response to death or disease progression), clinical benefit rate (the proportion of patients with a best overall response of complete response, partial response, or stable disease for at least 24 weeks), and safety.

The results for progression-free survival in the interim analysis have been reported previously, with a median follow-up of 15.5 months.20 Here, we primarily present the prespecified final analysis of progression-free survival, reporting of overall survival, objective response, duration of response, and safety, with additional assessment of long term survival outcomes.

sec.title: Statistical analysis
sec.p: Based on an assumption of a median progression-free survival of 12.5 months with trastuzumab and docetaxel, the study aimed to have 410 investigator assessed progression-free survival events to provide 80% power to detect a four month increase with the pyrotinib plus trastuzumab and docetaxel regimen (16.5 months, hazard ratio 0.76), at a one sided significance level of 0.025 for superiority. Considering a dropout rate of about 15%, the study planned to enrol a total of 590 patients. Prespecified interim analysis and final analysis of progression-free survival were to be conducted when about 275 events (67% of the expected events) and 410 events had occurred, respectively, and the superiority boundaries were set following the Lan-DeMets (O’Brien-Fleming) alpha spending function. The superiority boundary of progression-free survival was crossed at the interim analysis and no formal hypothesis testing on overall survival was prespecified, so the results reported in this paper, for both progression-free survival and overall survival, are with nominal one sided P values.

Efficacy was evaluated in the full analysis set, which included all randomised patients, whereas safety was assessed in the safety set, comprising all randomised patients who received at least one dose of the study drugs. The Kaplan-Meier method was used to estimate the time-to-event endpoints, including progression-free survival, overall survival, and duration of response, and the Brookmeyer Crowley method was used to calculate the corresponding 95% confidence intervals (CIs). The Kaplan-Meier method was also used to estimate the survival rates for progression-free survival and overall survival, with differences between groups assessed using the stratified log-rank test, and hazard ratios and corresponding 95% CIs determined using the stratified Cox proportional hazards model. We compared the proportions of overall responses and clinical benefits between groups using the Cochran-Mantel-Haenszel method with stratification factors and estimated the 95% CI using the Wald method. Subgroup analysis for progression-free survival was conducted using the unstratified Cox proportional hazards model. Follow-up duration was calculated from the time of randomisation until the last available survival date or death. The median follow-up time was calculated using descriptive statistical methods. All statistical analyses were performed using SAS (SAS Institute), version 9.4 or higher. Additional details are provided in the statistical analysis plan (see supplementary appendix).

sec.title: Patient and public involvement
sec.p: Participants were aware of the purpose and content of this trial during recruitment, although they were not involved in the initial design of the trial. Owing to the confidentiality of clinical data, patients did not participate in the subsequent statistical analysis or writing of the manuscript. The results were, however, communicated to patients who expressed an interest during clinic visits.

sec.title: Patients
sec.p: Out of the 590 eligible participants, 297 patients were assigned to the pyrotinib group (receiving pyrotinib plus trastuzumab and docetaxel) and 293 to the placebo group (receiving placebo plus trastuzumab and docetaxel). All patients in both groups received at least one dose of the treatment and were included in both the full analysis set and the safety set. Previous reports have indicated that the baseline characteristics of participants were generally similar between the two groups.20

The final analysis of progression-free survival was conducted with a data cut-off point of 30 April 2024, which was two years after the interim analysis cut-off date for investigator assessed progression-free survival. The median follow-up period was 35.7 months (interquartile range (IQR) 28.5-43.4) in the pyrotinib group and 34.3 months (27.5-42.4) in the placebo group. The median number of treatment cycles was 26 (IQR 13-50) in the pyrotinib group and 15 (10-26) in the placebo group. The median number of treatment cycles with trastuzumab was 24 (IQR 12-48) in the pyrotinib group and 14 (9-24) in the placebo group and with docetaxel was 8 (7-10) and 8 (6-12), respectively.

By the data cut-off point, 91 (31%) patients in the pyrotinib group and 26 (9%) in the placebo group were still undergoing treatment (fig 1). The primary reason for treatment discontinuation in both groups was radiological progression (152 (51%) patients in the pyrotinib group and 224 (76%) in the placebo group). Overall, 154 (52%) patients in the pyrotinib group and 222 (76%) in the placebo group received post-discontinuation treatments (see supplementary table S1). The proportion of patients receiving pyrotinib, trastuzumab, pertuzumab, or anti-HER2 antibody-drug conjugate after discontinuation of study treatment in the pyrotinib group and placebo group was, respectively, 17% (n=50) v 50% (n=146), 25% (n=74) v 25% (n=72), 15% (n=44) v 13% (n=39), and 16% (n=48) v 24% (n=70), respectively.

caption.p: Trial profile of patients with human epidermal growth factor receptor 2 positive metastatic breast cancer assigned to pyrotinib or placebo combined with trastuzumab and docetaxel

sec.p: By 30 May 2025, the data cut-off for long term survival analysis, the median follow-up duration was 45.5 months overall, 46.5 months (IQR 36-55) in the pyrotinib group, and 44.6 months (31-53) in the placebo group. At the data cut-off point, 75 (25%) of patients in the pyrotinib group and 19 (6%) in the placebo group were still receiving study treatment. Supplementary table S2 details the post-discontinuation treatments as of this data cut-off point.

sec.title: Efficacy
sec.p: As of 30 April 2024, 166 (56%) investigator assessed progression-free survival events occurred in the pyrotinib group and 242 (83%) in the placebo group. The pyrotinib group showed a sustained benefit in investigator assessed progression-free survival compared with the placebo group, with a median of 22.1 months (95% CI 19.3 to 27.8) versus 10.5 months (95% CI 9.5 to 12.4), and a hazard ratio of 0.44 (95% CI 0.36 to 0.53; nominal one sided P<0.001; fig 2). The three year progression-free survival rates were 40% (95% CI 34% to 46%) in the pyrotinib group and 10% (95% CI 6% to 14%) in the placebo group. Pyrotinib combination treatment showed a consistent progression-free survival benefit across all protocol prespecified subgroups (fig 3). In the subgroup of patients with previous neoadjuvant or adjuvant trastuzumab treatment (hazard ratio 0.26, 95% CI 0.14 to 0.46), without previous neoadjuvant or adjuvant trastuzumab (0.46, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.57), with a treatment-free interval of 12 months or more to less than 24 months for previous adjuvant treatment (0.21, 95% CI 0.11 to 0.43), and with a treatment-free interval of 24 months or more for previous adjuvant therapy (0.53, 95% CI 0.37 to 0.75), the benefits of progression-free survival with pyrotinib combination treatment were unchanged from the previous interim analysis (see supplementary figures S1 and S2).

sec.p: At the long term analysis cut-off point of 30 May 2025, the pyrotinib combination showed consistent and prolonged investigator assessed progression-free survival benefit (0.44, 95% CI 0.36 to 0.54; nominal one sided P<0.001; fig 4). The progression-free survival rates in the pyrotinib group and placebo group were, respectively, 40% and 10% at three years, 32% and 8% at four years, and 29% and 4% at five years. Additionally, the benefits in progression-free survival with pyrotinib combination treatment were consistent across nearly all analysed subgroups (see supplementary figure S3). Notably, for patients with previous neoadjuvant or adjuvant trastuzumab treatment, median progression-free survival was 62.8 months (95% CI 19.2 to not evaluable) in the pyrotinib group compared with 10.4 months (6.4 to 13.2) in the placebo group (see supplementary figure S1C).

sec.p: Although crossover was not allowed in this study, 50% (n=146) of patients in the control group received a treatment regimen containing pyrotinib after completing the study treatment (see supplementary table S1). By 30 April 2024, 59 (20%) deaths were reported in the pyrotinib group and 87 (30%) in the placebo group. The pyrotinib group showed superior overall survival compared with the placebo group (hazard ratio 0.64 (95% CI 0.46 to 0.89); nominal one sided P=0.004; fig 5, fig 6), and neither group reached the median overall survival. The overall survival rates in the pyrotinib group and placebo group were, respectively, 97% (95% CI 94% to 98%) and 95% (95% CI 91% to 97%) at one year, 89% (85% to 92%) and 84% (79% to 88%) at two years, 81% (76% to 85%) and 72% (67% to 77%) at three years, and 75% (67% to 81%) and 64% (57% to 71%) at four years.

sec.p: In the long term survival analysis, 85 deaths (29%) occurred in the pyrotinib group and 108 (37%) in the placebo group by 30 May 2025. Overall survival was longer in the pyrotinib group compared with placebo group (hazard ratio 0.74 (95% CI 0.56 to 0.98); nominal one sided P=0.02; fig 7). Neither group reached the median overall survival. Overall survival rates in the pyrotinib group and placebo group were, respectively, 80% and 72% at three years, 73% and 63.5% at four years, and 66% and 58.5% at five years. Subgroup analyses of overall survival were generally consistent with the results for all patients (see supplementary figure S4).

sec.p: The tumour response benefit associated with pyrotinib combination treatment was also maintained. Specifically, 84% (n=250, 95% CI 80% to 88%) of patients in the pyrotinib group and 72% (n=210, 66% to 77%) in the placebo group achieved an objective response as assessed by an investigator, and 89% (n=263, 84% to 92%) and 81% (n=237, 76% to 85%) of patients achieved clinical benefit, respectively (table 1). By 30 April 2024, 98 (39%) of the 250 responses in the pyrotinib group and 26 (12%) of the 210 responses in the placebo group were ongoing. The estimated median duration of response per investigator was 22.3 months (95% CI 17.9 to 29.3) in the pyrotinib group and 10.4 months (95% CI 8.4 to 12.4) in the placebo group.

sec.title: Safety
sec.p: The safety data cut-off point was 30 April 2024. The safety profiles observed in the updated analysis remained consistent with those reported in the previous interim analysis for frequency, severity, and specificity.20 No new safety signals were identified during the extended follow-up period.

The incidence of treatment related adverse events was 100% (n=297) in the pyrotinib group and 100% (n=292) in the placebo group, with diarrhoea (99% v 54%) and decreased white blood cell count (85% v 85%) being the most common reported events (table 2). A total of 91% (n=270) of the patients in the pyrotinib group and 77% (n=227) in the placebo group experienced grade 3 or higher treatment related adverse events, with decreased neutrophil count (63% v 65%), decreased white blood cell count (53% v 51%), and diarrhoea (48% v 4%) being the most prevalent. Furthermore, 81 (27%) patients in the pyrotinib group and 22 (8%) in the placebo group had treatment related serious adverse events, with diarrhoea (5% v 0%), increased alanine aminotransferase levels (3% v 1%), and febrile neutropenia (3% v 2%) being the most frequent (see supplementary table S3). After discontinuation of docetaxel, the incidence of all adverse events decreased considerably; grade 3 adverse events were rare (table 2 and supplementary table S4).

sec.p: Treatment related adverse events that led to dose reduction of any component were reported in 82 (28%) patients in the pyrotinib group and nine (3%) in the placebo group. Treatment interruptions of any component due to treatment related adverse events occurred in 181 (61%) patients in the pyrotinib group and 77 (26%) in the placebo group. Additionally, discontinuation of treatment of any component due to treatment related adverse events was noted in 45 (15%) patients in the pyrotinib group and 22 (8%) in the placebo group (see supplementary table S5). No treatment related deaths occurred in the pyrotinib group, whereas one (diabetic hyperosmolar coma) occurred in the placebo group. No treatment related death has been reported since the interim analysis.

One common adverse event associated with pyrotinib treatment is diarrhoea, which occurred more frequently in the pyrotinib group compared with the placebo group, both overall and at grade 3 severity, as observed in both the previous interim analysis and the current updated analysis. Diarrhoea of any grade was reported in 99% (n=293) of patients in the pyrotinib group and 55% (n=162) in the placebo group, with most being grade 1-2. Grade 3 diarrhoea was observed in 48% (n=142) of patients in the pyrotinib group and only 4% (n=13) in the placebo group (see supplementary table S6), and grade 4 or 5 diarrhoea was not reported. Grade 3 diarrhoea predominantly occurred during the initial cycle of treatment (36% (n=107) v 1% (n=2) in the pyrotinib and placebo groups, respectively), with a notable decrease in occurrence during subsequent cycles. The median time to onset of grade 3 diarrhoea was 9.0 days (IQR 6.0-20.0) in the pyrotinib group compared with 88.0 days (IQR 28.0-198.0) in the placebo group. The median duration of grade 3 diarrhoea was 1.0 day (IQR 1.0-1.0) in both treatment groups, with a median cumulative duration of 3.0 days (IQR 2.0-7.0) in the pyrotinib group and 1.0 day (IQR 1.0-2.0) in the placebo group. Loperamide hydrochloride prophylaxis was recommended per protocol, with pyrotinib dose reductions (18%, n=52/297) or treatment interruptions (25%, 75/297) implemented for persistent toxicity. No patients discontinued the study treatment due to grade 3 diarrhoea in either treatment group. After docetaxel had been discontinued, the incidence of any grade diarrhoea decreased from 98% (245/249) to 80% (199/249) in the pyrotinib group and from 54% (121/226) to 15% (35/226) in the placebo group. Similarly, incidence of grade 3 diarrhoea declined from 46% (115/249) to 16% (40/249) in the pyrotinib group and from 3% (7/226) to 0.4% (1/226) in the placebo group (see supplementary table S7).
No heart failure was observed in the pyrotinib group, but decreased ejection fraction occurred in 2% (6/297) of patients and left ventricular dysfunction in 1% (2/297; see supplementary table S8).

sec.title: Discussion
sec.p: The prespecified final analysis for progression-free survival in phase 3 of the PHILA trial showed that a regimen of pyrotinib, trastuzumab, and docetaxel prolonged progression-free survival compared with a regimen of placebo, trastuzumab, and docetaxel in patients with HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer (median 22.1 months v 10.5 months; hazard ratio 0.44; nominal one sided P<0.001). Pyrotinib, trastuzumab, and docetaxel treatment was associated with a 36% reduction in the risk of death (hazard ratio 0.64) compared with placebo, trastuzumab, and docetaxel. Notably, after five years of treatment, 66% of patients survived and 30% did not experience disease progression or death. The safety profile of the pyrotinib based regimen remained consistent with that reported in the previous interim analysis, showing grade ≥3 diarrhoea in 48% of patients (effectively controlled using loperamide hydrochloride and dose modifications) alongside docetaxel induced haematological adverse effects, over a median follow-up of 35.9 months.20 This updated analysis further reinforces the pyrotinib based regimen as an efficacious strategy for the initial treatment of patients with HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer.

sec.title: Comparison with other studies
sec.p: In the full analysis population, the progression-free survival benefit of pyrotinib, trastuzumab, and docetaxel in the final analysis was consistent with that reported in the interim analyses. This benefit persisted through 45.5 months of median follow-up, underscoring the durability of response with the pyrotinib based regimen. Subgroup analyses of progression-free survival from the final analysis further supported the efficacy of this regimen across various patient populations. The sustained benefit for progression-free survival across all protocol prespecified subgroups emphasised the broad applicability of this regimen in patients with HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer. In those who had previously received trastuzumab, either as neoadjuvant or adjuvant treatment, a progression-free survival benefit (hazard ratio 0.26) similar to the overall study population was observed, suggesting that for patients previously treated with trastuzumab, a regimen containing pyrotinib in patients with metastatic disease is more likely to achieve greater progression-free survival benefit compared with those with no history of trastuzumab treatment. Furthermore, subgroup analyses of progression-free survival based on treatment-free interval indicated that for those with disease progression within 12 to 24 months of adjuvant treatment, a pyrotinib based regimen was more favourable in reducing the risk of progression compared with those with disease progression after 24 months of adjuvant treatment. A regimen containing pyrotinib delayed time to onset of brain metastasis, which might be partially attributed to dual HER2 inhibition strategy using a combination of a small molecule tyrosine kinase inhibitor and monoclonal antibody. Among patients who developed brain metastases, the median time to onset was 16.6 months (IQR 13-28) in the pyrotinib group (n=34) compared with 9.1 months (IQR 8-14) in the placebo group (n=30).

The overall survival data also indicate a strong survival benefit with the pyrotinib based regimen over the placebo based regimen, although neither treatment group reached the median overall survival. The Kaplan-Meier curves of the two treatment groups showed an early separation, and the separation continued over time, which was also reflected by the hazard ratio for overall survival, indicating a 26% reduction in the risk of death at the median follow-up of 45.5 months. The hazard ratio for overall survival in the pyrotinib group (0.74) was comparable to the hazard ratio reported for the pertuzumab arm (0.68) in the CLEOPATRA study.11 Notably, median overall survival in the current trial was not reached in the placebo group at 45.5 months of median follow-up, whereas the CLEOPATRA study reported a median overall survival of 37.6 months in the placebo group at a median follow-up of 30 months.8 The difference in the timing of the reported overall survival results may be attributed to the differences in subsequent treatments between trials. In the control arm of the current study, more than 25% of patients received anti-HER2 antibody-drug conjugates after disease progression. In the CLEOPATRA study, however, no antibody-drug conjugates were used.10 Although crossover was not allowed in the current study, this high rate of post-discontinuation HER2 directed treatment in the control arm likely attenuated the overall survival difference between groups. Nevertheless, a clear trend of benefit in overall survival rates at four and five years was still observed in the current study (73% v 64% at four years, 66% v 59% at five years). This was also evident in the CLEOPATRA study (58% v 45% at four years, 49% v 35% at five years).10 11 These data suggest that pyrotinib based treatment offers a competitive efficacy profile compared with established dual HER2 inhibition regimens in the initial treatment setting.

In terms of safety, the adverse event profile in the current study was consistent with previous findings in the interim analysis,20 and it aligned with the established safety profile of individual agents.14 15 17 No new safety signals were identified during the extended follow-up period, indicating the continued safety and tolerability of pyrotinib in combination with trastuzumab and docetaxel. After the interim analysis, only six (2.4%) new treatment related serious adverse events in the pyrotinib group and one (0.6%) in the placebo group were reported. The most common adverse event with the pyrotinib based regimen was diarrhoea,22 with 48% of patients experiencing grade 3 diarrhoea in the pyrotinib group, which predominantly occurred during the initial treatment cycle. The high rate observed in this study could be attributed to the unique pharmacodynamics of pyrotinib, which targets multiple HER receptors. However, prophylactic loperamide hydrochloride and dose adjustments effectively managed these events,23 24 25 resulting in no discontinuations due to grade 3 diarrhoea. Although pyrotinib was associated with longer treatment duration (median 26 cycles), docetaxel showed a median of eight cycles, consistent with its known toxicity profile and reflecting effective management of toxicity.11 After discontinuation of docetaxel, a noticeable improvement in overall safety was observed in patients, with a reduction in diarrhoea incidence (grade 3 diarrhoea decreased from 46% to 16% in the pyrotinib group). The frequent occurrence of grade 3 or higher treatment related adverse events in both study groups was mainly due to the haematological toxicities of docetaxel, masking adverse events associated with pyrotinib. Leukopoietic agents can be used to effectively manage docetaxel induced haematological adverse events. Cardiac toxicity, an adverse event commonly associated with HER2 targeted treatments, was low, with no statistically significant differences between the pyrotinib and control groups in terms of decreased ejection fraction (2.0% v 0.7%).

sec.title: Limitations of this study
sec.p: One of the major limitations of this study was the absence of a control group using pertuzumab-trastuzumab combination treatment. Although pertuzumab plus trastuzumab and docetaxel had been approved for the initial treatment of HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer in North America (2012) and Europe (2013) based on the CLEOPATRA study, it was not approved in China when the current study was designed in 2018. Caution is needed when comparing trials of pertuzumab-trastuzumab combination treatments. Additionally, identifying biomarkers that predict response and resistance to pyrotinib based regimens could enable more personalised treatment approaches and improve patient outcomes. The median overall survival was not reached in either study group, and long term follow-up studies are essential to fully understand the survival benefits.

sec.title: Conclusions
sec.p: The final analysis reinforces the efficacy and safety of pyrotinib in combination with trastuzumab and docetaxel for the initial treatment ofHER2 positive metastatic breast cancer. The long term analysis confirmed that the improvements in overall survival and progression-free survival were maintained after 45.5 months of median follow-up, suggesting the utility of dual anti-HER2 regimen (pyrotinib plus trastuzumab) as an established treatment strategy for this patient population.

sec.title: What is already known on this topic

list-item.p: Dual blockade of HER2 (human epidermal growth factor receptor 2) provides comprehensive inhibition of signalling, resulting in greater antitumour activity than either agent alone

The combination of pertuzumab, trastuzumab, and docetaxel has been established as the standard initial treatment for HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer, statistically significantly improving progression-free survival and overall survival
Pyrotinib, trastuzumab, and docetaxel showed superiority in improving progression-free survival in patients with untreated HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer, with an acceptable safety profile
Pyrotinib, trastuzumab, and docetaxel showed overall survival benefit in untreated patients with HER2 positive metastatic breast cancer despite post-discontinuation of anti-HER2 treatments
The improvement of progression-free survival with pyrotinib, trastuzumab, and docetaxel shown in previous analyses was maintained during long term follow-up
The finding of long term analysis reinforced the use of dual anti-HER2 regimen (pyrotinib plus trastuzumab) as an established treatment strategy for this patient population
